learn.hook: Before a cricket toss, everyone knows the possible outcomes — heads or tails — but no one knows which. That's a random experiment, and probability measures our uncertainty about it.
points: A random experiment has more than one possible outcome, and the outcome cannot be predicted in advance. The set of all outcomes is the sample space S.

Classical probability: P(E) = (number of favourable outcomes)/(total number of outcomes), when all outcomes are equally likely. It fails when outcomes are not equally likely or infinitely many, which is why we need the axiomatic approach.
An event is a subset of the sample space. E.g. 'an even number' on a die is E = {2, 4, 6} ⊆ S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
The event E occurs if the actual outcome ω belongs to E.
Toss a coin twice: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; 'exactly one head' = {HT, TH}.

example.q: A die is thrown. Write the sample space and the event 'a number greater than 4'. If the die shows 6, does this event occur?

learn.reallife: IPL captains choose to bat or bowl after a toss, a random experiment with sample space {H, T}; analysts later study how often the toss winner wins the match.

topics.title: Impossible, sure, simple, compound and complementary events

learn.hook: Rolling a 7 on a normal die can never happen; rolling a number below 7 always happens. Events come in types, and naming them makes problems easy.
points: Impossible event: ∅ (no outcome), e.g. 'a 7 on a die'. Sure event: S itself, e.g. 'a number less than 7'.
Simple (elementary) event: exactly one sample point, e.g. {4}.
Compound event: more than one sample point, e.g. 'an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
Complementary event 'not A': A′ = S − A = {ω ∈ S : ω ∉ A}.
Example: for a die, if A = {1, 2, 3}, then A′ = {4, 5, 6}.

example.q: Three coins are tossed. Let A = 'at least two heads'. Write A and A′.
steps: A′ = 'at most one head' = {HTT, THT, TTH, TTT}.
example.answer: A has 4 outcomes; A′ = {HTT, THT, TTH, TTT}

learn.reallife: Weather apps say '30% chance of rain'; the complementary event 'no rain' then has a 70% chance — complements in everyday use.

topics.title: Algebra of events: or, and, but not

learn.hook: 'Rain OR wind', 'rain AND wind', 'rain but NOT wind' — event language is set language in disguise.
points: 'A or B' = A ∪ B (at least one of them occurs). 'A and B' = A ∩ B (both occur).
'A but not B' = A − B = A ∩ B′.
A and B are mutually exclusive if A ∩ B = ∅: they cannot occur together.
E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ are exhaustive if E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ = S. If, in addition, they are pairwise disjoint, they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
Example with one die: A = {1, 3, 5} (odd) and B = {2, 4, 6} (even) are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

example.q: A die is thrown. A = 'prime number' = {2, 3, 5}, B = 'odd number' = {1, 3, 5}. Find A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A − B.

learn.reallife: An insurance company splits customers into mutually exclusive and exhaustive age groups so that each person falls into exactly one group.

topics.title: Axioms of probability and equally likely outcomes

learn.hook: Kolmogorov boiled all of probability down to three simple rules. Every formula you'll use follows from them.
points: Axiom 1: P(E) ≥ 0 for every event E. Axiom 2: P(S) = 1. Axiom 3: if E and F are mutually exclusive, P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F).
Consequences: P(∅) = 0, and 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.
For a finite sample space, assign P(ωᵢ) to each outcome with 0 ≤ P(ωᵢ) ≤ 1 and ΣP(ωᵢ) = 1. P(E) = sum of P(ωᵢ) over ωᵢ ∈ E.
An assignment is valid only if every value is between 0 and 1 and the values add up to 1.
If all n outcomes are equally likely, each has probability 1/n and P(E) = n(E)/n(S).

example.q: S = {ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, ω₄} with P(ω₁) = 0.1, P(ω₂) = 0.3, P(ω₃) = 0.4, P(ω₄) = 0.2. Is this valid? Find P({ω₂, ω₃}).

learn.reallife: A biased cricket coin (heads 0.6, tails 0.4) still obeys the axioms: each probability is non-negative and they add to 1.

topics.title: Addition rule and the complement rule

learn.hook: Probability of a king OR a heart? Not 4/52 + 13/52 — that counts the king of hearts twice. Subtract the overlap!
points: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) for any events A and B.
If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
Complement rule: P(not A) = P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
P(A but not B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B). P(neither A nor B) = P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).
Draw a Venn diagram: the three regions A only, both, B only add to P(A ∪ B).

example.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Find P(A ∪ B), P(A′ ∩ B′) and P(A but not B).

learn.hook: What are your chances of winning a lottery where you pick 6 numbers from 20? About 1 in 38,760. Combinations turn probability into counting.
points: P(E) = n(E)/n(S), where both counts are found with permutations or combinations.
Selections (committees, hands of cards, balls drawn together): use ⁿCᵣ for both n(E) and n(S).
Arrangements (letters, seating): use factorials or ⁿPᵣ for both counts.
'At least one' problems: P = 1 − P(none).
Read carefully whether order matters and whether drawing is with or without replacement.

example.q: A committee of 3 is chosen from 4 men and 6 women. Find the probability that it has exactly 2 women.

learn.reallife: State lotteries publish the odds 1/ⁿCᵣ; a lottery picking 6 of 20 numbers gives 1/38,760 — counting tells you the real chance.
